I want to be accurate about this, because I have heard it repeated wrongly. I did not ignore the alarm. I watched it for two minutes, I decided it was the sensor, and then I stopped watching it. Those are two different things and only one of them is what I did. What I did not do, and what I regret, is stop to read the fault code. Fifteen seconds. The code would have told me the fault was in the circuit and I would have called the engine room at three forty-three instead of at four fifty. And yes, I had been on watch for eleven hours, and no, I am not offering that as an explanation. Plenty of people do eleven hours and read the code. I remember signing the checklist. I do not remember checking a single item on it, and I have said so from the first interview.

Every checklist starts as a procedure and ends as a signature, and the interval is usually about two years. The first time a form is used, somebody walks the deck with it. The fiftieth time, somebody signs it in the office because he already knows what it says. And he does know. That is the uncomfortable part: the people who sign without checking are usually the ones who understand the system best. So we stopped adding items. Adding items is what everybody tries first, and it makes the problem worse, because the longer the form the faster it is signed. What we do now is change one item every month, without announcing which. If you have actually worked through the list, you notice. If you have remembered to sign it, you do not.
